scenes.title: Refusals: check before you read
scenes.body: If `stop_reason` is `"refusal"`, the model declined and the content may be empty. Check it **before** reading the text. Optionally, the API can automatically retry a declined request on another model (`fallbacks`), which our project turns on.

scenes.question: Your code parses `response.content[0].text` as JSON and it fails on a long reply. What should you check first?
scenes.explain: A reply cut off at `max_tokens` ends mid-JSON. Check `stop_reason`, raise the limit, or ask for less.

items.text: `stop_reason` tells you if the reply is complete. Check it.

captions.text: Getting a reply is easy.
Getting a reply your program can rely on takes more care.
In this lesson you'll control how long replies are, show them as they're generated,
get structured JSON instead of free text, and handle the cases where the model stops
early.
You'll use max tokens, and check the stop reason every time.
Stream replies for a responsive interface.
Get validated JSON with structured outputs.
And handle refusals safely.
Every response tells you why it ended.
End turn means the model finished its answer naturally.
Max tokens means it hit your limit and was cut off, possibly mid-sentence.
Refusal means the model declined the request for safety reasons.
Stop sequence means it produced one of the custom stop strings you supplied.
Tool use means it wants to run one of your tools.
That's the heart of agents, in Module 5.
And pause turn means a long agentic turn paused, and you can continue it.
We ask the same question twice, once with a generous limit and once with only
fifteen tokens.
And we check the stop reason.
A cut-off reply looks like a normal string, so if you don't check, you'll silently
show users half an answer, or try to parse half a JSON document.
With a thousand tokens, end turn.
With fifteen, the stop reason is max tokens, and exactly fifteen output tokens were
used.
The model doesn't plan to fit the limit.
It's simply stopped.
So set max tokens high enough for the job, and treat max tokens as the stop reason
that needs handling.
Don't lowball it to save money.
A truncated answer usually costs you a retry.
Remember that models generate one token at a time.
Without streaming, your program waits for the entire reply, with nothing on screen.
With streaming, the API sends pieces as they're generated, so text appears almost
immediately.
The total time is the same, but it feels far faster.
Streaming also avoids request timeouts on very long replies.
Messages dot stream takes exactly the same arguments as create, and is used as a
context manager with with.
Text stream yields small pieces of text as they arrive.
We print each one immediately, with flush equals True so it isn't held in a buffer.
And when the stream ends, get final message gives you the complete message object,
with its stop reason and usage, just like create.
In the video the pieces arrive instantly, because the fake API is local, but the
code path is the real streaming code: server-sent events, parsed by the SDK.
Agents constantly need machine-readable output: a quiz, a plan, a tool decision.
Just asking for JSON in the prompt is fragile.
Extra words, wrong keys, or broken JSON can slip through.
Structured outputs fix this.
You pass a JSON schema, and the API constrains the reply to valid JSON for that
schema.
With a Pydantic class, the SDK builds the schema and parses the reply into a Python
object for you.
First, describe the shape with Pydantic classes: a question has text, four options,
the index of the right answer, and an explanation.
A quiz has a topic and a list of questions.
Pydantic gets a full lesson in Module 3.
For now, read these as typed dataclasses.
These Field constraints say exactly four options and an index from zero to three.
The API's schema support is limited, so the SDK moves those limits into the field
descriptions, and then checks them itself when the reply arrives.
Then call messages dot parse instead of create, with output format set to the class.
Parsed output is a real, validated Quiz object, so you use attributes instead of
digging through dictionaries.
The offline fake returns schema-valid placeholder questions, and they come back as a
real Quiz object.
If a reply doesn't fit the schema, the SDK raises a validation error instead of
handing you bad data.
Last case: refusals.
If the stop reason is refusal, the model declined the request for safety reasons,
and the content may be empty.
So check the stop reason before you read the text.
On current models, the API can also automatically re-run a declined request on
another model, a feature called fallbacks.
Our project turns it on, and you'll see the code in lesson six.
Quick check.
Your code parses the reply as JSON, and it fails on a long reply.
What should you check first?
Whether the stop reason is max tokens.
A cut-off reply ends in the middle of the JSON.
The stop reason tells you whether the reply is complete.
Always check it.
Stream for responsive output.
Use structured outputs, with messages dot parse, for validated JSON.
And handle refusals before reading the content.
